Regulation of MAPT (Tau) Translation in Basal Forebrain Axons

\vspace{0.5cm}

By ELINA NEMTSOV

\vspace{1cm}

Dissertation Director:\\

Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons (BFCNs) provide extensive cholinergic innervation to both the hippocampus and the cerebral cortex. They are a unique population of cells, both in their expression of the p75 neurotrophin receptor (p75NTR)—not only during neurogenesis but throughout adulthood—and in their expression of all three Trk receptors (TrkA, TrkB, and TrkC). The Trk receptors have a higher affinity for mature neurotrophins and signal for cell growth and survival, whereas p75NTR has a higher affinity for proneurotrophins and, when it binds its ligand, can signal for degeneration and cell death depending on the context.

Traumatic brain injury (TBI) involves more than the focal, mechanical damage at the site of injury that kills cells directly. The inflammatory reaction that follows the injury induces an elevation of proNGF, which can bind p75NTR on the axon terminals of the BFCNs that project to the injury site. The degeneration of these BFCNs is therefore not caused by direct mechanical damage to their cell bodies but is initiated distally, at the axon terminals.

Previous work from our lab showed that p75NTR activation at BFCN axon terminals triggers local protein synthesis and retrograde transport of degenerative signals, and that both processes are required for axonal fragmentation and neuronal death. Proteomic analysis of the newly synthesized proteins in the axonal compartment following proNGF treatment identified tau (MAPT) and amyloid precursor protein (APP) among the most statistically significant upregulated newly synthesized proteins, and showed that blocking the increase in newly synthesized APP prevents axonal degeneration and neuronal death. The goal of the present study is to investigate the role of tau in p75NTR-induced axonal degeneration.
